title: How To Use The Preview Strategy To Improve Behavior e-behavior/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin introduces the 'preview strategy,' a simple, low-effort technique for boosting student engagement without relying on external rewards. The method involves identifying the single most interesting element of an upcoming lesson and briefly highlighting it for students beforehand, piquing their curiosity. He walks through a step-by-step process: searching lessons for a noteworthy 'one thing,' defining why it stands out, and delivering short, enthusiastic previews before each lesson and during the morning schedule walkthrough. He notes the strategy also requires a fairness caveat reminding students that participation depends on following classroom rules. Linsin frames the technique as a way to reignite joy in learning, arguing that when students look forward to lessons, misbehavior becomes far less likely.
points: The preview strategy works by identifying and briefly highlighting the single most interesting element of each lesson before teaching it.
It is intrinsic in nature and does not rely on prizes, praise, or external rewards to capture student interest.
Previews should be simple, brief, and spoken from the heart rather than formally scripted.
Previewing the daily schedule with several compelling highlights keeps students engaged rather than tuning out a routine recitation.
A behavior caveat should be included, reminding students that participation in exciting activities depends on following classroom rules.
quotes: The preview strategy is intrinsic in nature and involves a simple piquing of your students’ interest in the activities you have planned for the day.

When you’re looking over your lesson plans before school, or better yet, when you’re first creating them, search for that “one thing” in each lesson that is potentially most interesting to your students.
The most effective teachers are able to provide for their students compelling reasons why they should pay attention, why they should lean forward and care about what they’re about to learn.
Unless you have a learning environment your students enjoy and look forward to coming to every day, then there isn’t a rule or consequence in the world that is likely to help.
So look for that “one thing” in every lesson. Reignite the joy of learning for your students.
One of the great things about the preview strategy is that it will cause you to really sell what you’re teaching.
